For three decades the web was built for human eyes. Pages were laid out in columns and grids, decorated with imagery and motion, and tuned so that a person scanning a screen could find what they needed. That assumption is quietly breaking down. A growing share of web traffic now comes not from people but from automated agents acting on their behalf, and those agents do not see pixels at all.

What an automated reader wants is not a rendered layout but the underlying semantic meaning of a document: its headings, its prose, the relationships between sections, and the links that connect one resource to the next. Stylesheets, sprite sheets, and animation timelines are pure overhead to such a consumer. They add weight and ambiguity without adding any information the reader can use.

This is why tooling that extracts structured data from ordinary pages has become so valuable. By discarding presentational scaffolding and keeping only the content that carries meaning, such tools hand a model a compact, faithful representation of a page. The result reads less like a screenshot and more like a clean document, which is exactly the form an agent reasons over most reliably.

None of this means the visual web disappears. People will keep browsing with their eyes for a long time yet. But alongside that human web, a second, machine facing web is taking shape, and it is organized around semantics rather than appearance. Building for that reader is a different discipline, and it starts by throwing away almost everything a designer spent years learning to add.
